episodes.170555: An abundant amount of moisture in the atmosphere led to another very active monsoon day for northern and central New Mexico on July 29, 2022. Thunderstorms developed early in the day across the high terrain areas before becoming more widespread as the day progressed. Heavy rain was common with these thunderstorms, especially on the Calf Canyon burn scar which reported more burn scar flash flooding and debris flow. The Gallup area also received heavy rainfall which forced the closure of a few area roadways. Meanwhile, a few thunderstorms across the eastern plains briefly turned strong to severe which prompted a few Severe Thunderstorm Warnings. One thunderstorm near Logan looked like it was producing baseball size hail according to radar, but a trained spotter only reported quarter size hail.
episodes.170556: The end of July continued to be busy for meteorologists at the Albuquerque National Weather Service Office as numerous thunderstorms impacted the area on July 30, 2022. With well above normal moisture available in the atmosphere, these thunderstorms were robust and very capable of producing heavy rainfall. Several flash flooding reports were received, including in the Rio Rancho and Edgewood areas.
episodes.170611: Thunderstorms developed along a weak cold front during the midday hours and knocked down trees in parts of DeKalb County. Also, there was one report of flash flooding in the county.
episodes.170718: Abundant monsoon moisture remained over the Four Corners region. This led to another round of showers and thunderstorms across southeast Utah. Storms were slow moving and produced heavy rain. A debris flow occurred on the Pack Creek Fire burn scar as a result of a large amount of heavy rain in a short period of time.
episodes.170719: Abundant monsoon moisture remained over the Four Corners region. This led to another round of showers and thunderstorms across western Colorado. Storms were slow moving and produced heavy rain. Some storms produced localized debris flows in Pitkin and Ouray counties with flooding reported in Montrose County.
episodes.171293: Several days of monsoon thunderstorms impacted the mountains and High Desert in Southern California. The San Bernardino County Mountains were particularly hard hit. Torrential downpours led to flash flooding and debris flows, including over the El Dorado burn scar.
episodes.171823: A large cluster of thunderstorms developed in the early evening hours along a subtle boundary oriented west to east across Berkeley County. The thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.171912: A tropical upper-tropospheric trough (TUTT) low was moving westward across the northern Gulf of Mexico. This feature brought with it, abundant moisture throughout the column as well as a focus for storms to develop. As storms began to develop in the morning hours along coastal areas, one interacted with a sea/land-breeze boundary which resulted in a waterspout forming over Terrebonne Bay. It remained offshore.
episodes.171913: A tropical upper-tropospheric trough (TUTT) low was moving westward across the northern Gulf of Mexico. This feature brought with it, abundant moisture throughout the column as well as a focus for storms to develop. Heavy rain and flash flooding occurred in St. Bernard Parish as the TUTT low moved into the area.
episodes.171976: A few thunderstorms became severe in late July on the 28th and 30th along a quasi-stationary boundary draped across northern sections of the state. Severe storms were mainly oriented along a west to east line adjacent to the frontal boundary.
episodes.172222: Heavy rainfall occurred during the late evening of the 29th into the early morning of the 30th as a low level jet interacted with a stalled front.  Several locations received over three inches of rain with some reporting six inches in a 3-4 hour period.
episodes.172297: Isolated strong thunderstorms developed late in the day and into the evening across parts of northern El Paso County. Heavy rain with localized flooding were the main hazards, especially on the east side of Colorado Springs and near the Palmer Divide.
episodes.172298: Thunderstorm development was isolated on this day, with only a few stronger storms producing heavy rainfall amounts.
episodes.172306: Two areas of severe weather developed during the evening and nighttime hours. The first area was along a cold front over northwest North Dakota, where strong thunderstorm wind gusts were the primary threat, with the strongest wind gust of 69 mph being reported at the Williston Airport in Williams County. The second area was over central North Dakota affecting Wells and Foster counties, where an area of thunderstorms produced strong thunderstorm winds and some large hail. The strongest reported wind gust in this area was 61 mph at the Carrington Airport in Foster County, while one inch diameter hail fell to the west of Hurdsfield in Wells County.
episodes.172307: A mid-level disturbance tracked east across the Midwest and Ohio Valley during the afternoon and evening. This disturbance allowed a cold front across Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana to approach central North Carolina during the evening and overnight. Ahead of the front, strong surface heating with a moist atmosphere, as well as a Piedmont trough, allowed isolated to scattered thunderstorms to develop in the late afternoon and evening across the western Piedmont, tracking east into the Sandhills and Coastal Plain overnight. A few of the storms led to downed trees and power lines.
episodes.172466: Daytime heating combined with divergence aloft associated with an easterly wave near the Arizona/New Mexico border promoted thunderstorm initiation across southeast Arizona during the afternoon of the 30th. Outflow boundaries generated from these thunderstorms raced northwest toward south-central Arizona, resulting in a dust storm in Pinal County where multiple instances of dense blowing dust less than 1/4 mile were reported. New thunderstorm development occurred along these boundaries with some thunderstorms becoming severe. Numerous instances of damaging winds were reported across the Phoenix area and down into northwest Pinal County, which included multiple downed trees and power poles. A very moist environment, with PWATs in excess of 1.80 allowed for thunderstorms to become efficient heavy rainfall producers. Rainfall amounts upwards of around 1.50 within an hour were reported during the event. There were multiple reports of flash flooding across northern parts of the Phoenix area, leading to several water rescues and making some roads impassable. Flash flooding also led to water and mud entering some apartments in north Phoenix causing extensive water damage. Isolated flash flooding occurred across Pinal, Gila, and Yuma Counties. No injuries were reported with this event.
episodes.172502: A strong upper-level ridge set up across the western U.S. with broad ridging extending eastward across the Ark-La-Tex region. However, slight weakening along the eastern extent of the ridge allowed for convection to become more likely with diurnal heating. At the surface, a weak frontal boundary located from along the middle Red River Valley eastward into central Arkansas had become nearly stationary. Along and south of the boundary, plentiful moisture characteristic of dew points mainly in the lower 70s were noted. Some lingering outflow boundaries were also present from earlier convection, and these features combined to help trigger an isolated severe thunderstorm during the early evening hours in Webster Parish. This storm produced isolated damaging wind gusts just north of Minden.
episodes.172554: Daytime instability resulted in thunderstorms that developed across portions of the Texas Panhandle. Severe wind gusts were reported across the southern Texas Panhandle, including some structural damage.
episodes.172563: Between July 25th and July 30th, 2022, several complexes of training thunderstorms developed south of I-64 and brought heavy rain, deadly flash flooding, and devastating river flooding to eastern Kentucky and central Appalachia. These thunderstorms, at times, caused rainfall rates in excess of 4/hr across complex terrain that led to widespread devastating impacts. While it did not rain continuously during this 4-day stretch, the overwhelming amounts of rain and resultant flooding led to 39 deaths and widespread catastrophic damage. Entire homes and parts of some communities were swept away by flood waters, leading to costly damage to infrastructure in the region. Over 600 helicopter rescues and countless swift water rescues by boat were needed to evacuate people who were trapped by the quickly-rising flood waters. In total, 24 Flash Flood Warnings were issued between July 26th and July 30th. Between the evening of July 27th and the mid-morning hours on July 28th (the peak of the event), 13 warnings were issued, 3 of which were upgraded to a Flash Flood Emergency.||Radar-based rainfall estimates suggest that upwards of 14-16 of rain fell during this 5-day period in a narrow swath, with many more locations receiving 6-10 of rain. Most of this rain fell during the night of July 27th into the morning of July 28th, which is when the most devastating impacts were felt. The highest totals occurred across an axis that stretches from northern Clay and southern Owsley counties, east through southern Breathitt and northern Leslie counties, into Perry, Knott and Letcher counties. The highest rainfall total report was from southern Knott County, where 14.00 fell between July 25th and July 29th. This site, a cooperative (COOP) observer at Carr Creek Lake, reported 6.71 from 7am July 28th to 7am July 29th, following a report of 6.50 at that site on the previous day. Another COOP site in Buckhorn reported 8.00 of rain for the 24-hour period ending 7am on July 28th. The rainfall total in Buckhorn from July 25th to July 29th was 11.76. These rainfall values occurring in such a short period of time are incredibly rare: there is less than a 1 in 1000 chance for this much rainfall over five days in a given year.||The incredible rainfall also led to significant rises and flooding on many rivers in eastern Kentucky including on the main stem of the Kentucky River; North, Middle and South forks of the Kentucky River; Red River and Licking River. At Whitesburg, the North Fork of the Kentucky River swelled well above major flood stage, reaching close to 21' before gauge failure (the previous flood of record was 14.7' in 1957). The North Fork of the Kentucky River at Jackson also reached major flood, setting a new record crest of 43.47' (the previous record was 43.1' set in 1939). The river flooding caused a second round of destruction for communities in the region, and caused flooding in downstream areas that did not receive as much rainfall.||*Note* Given the widespread nature and severity of this event - any dollar amount estimated by storm data will not do the event as a whole justice. Since eastern KY was a national declaration, FEMA will be doing a full cost assessment. Will use this data once available for total monetary amounts of damage.||Visit www.weather.gov/jkl/July2022Flooding for more information on the event, as well as pictures and videos of the flooding and damage.
episodes.172626: A large dust devil was video'd in Downey on July 29th.
episodes.172645: A push of monsoonal moisture resulted in sporadic flash flooding and isolated microbursts for the end of the month of July.
episodes.172689: Scattered thunderstorms moved northwest across southeast Arizona during the afternoon and evening. Storms caused wind damage to trees and produced flash flooding across northern parts of the Tucson Metro area.
episodes.172877: Deep monsoon moisture remained over northern Arizona with thunderstorms, heavy rain, and flash flooding.
episodes.172913: The stormy period which began on the 24th continued to bring severe weather and flash flooding through the end of the month.

episodes.172930: Deep monsoon moisture allowed the formation of thunderstorms with heavy rain and flash flooding across northern Arizona.
episodes.172960: Scattered thunderstorms developed over upstate South Carolina during the late afternoon. A couple of severe storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in Anderson County.
episodes.172963: Scattered thunderstorms developed over northeast Georgia during the late afternoon. An isolated severe storm produced brief damaging wind gusts in Hart County.
episodes.173071: A surface boundary sagged southward during the afternoon of July 29th and served as a catalyst for development of isolated strong to severe storms through July 30th across portions of North Georgia, including the Atlanta metro.  These storms produced isolated reports of trees down causing structural damage and flash flooding.

events.narrative: A large dust devil was video'd in Downey on July 29th and posted on facebook.
Peyton Highway flooded five miles north of Peyton.
Rangers at Zion National Park reported flash flooding in Pine Creek and side canyons off of Bridge Mountain due to excessive rainfall in the region.
A video of flash flooding three miles north of Fort Defiance was posted on social media.
Heavy rainfall of 2.50 inches.
Intersection of Meridian and Londonderry flooded 6-8 inches deep.
Power outages were caused by fallen trees near the intersection of Ortega Road and Windsor Place.
Heavy rainfall of 1.75 inches. Fell in 30 minutes.
Wooten Road flooded just north of Platte Avenue.
Hwy 190 was impassable in spots between Beatty Junction and Furnace Creek Wash Rd.
The intersection of Wilson Rd and East St was flooded.

Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar caused flash flooding and debris flow with a rock slide on County Road 65 near the E.V. Campground. Three people were rescued from flooding in this area. Damages are estimated.

Water over a few roads in the Kilpatrick Community, such as AL Highway 68 near County Road 478 and County Road 179. Also County Road 24 and AL Highway 68. County Road 478 was barricaded by law enforcement. Depth of water unknown.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees, some of which blocked roads, landed on cars, and landed on apartment buildings.
West Main Street was covered with flood waters at the railroad underpass in Beattyville. Water was also over Lumber Street at the Valero Gas Station.

Heavy rain in portions of the headwaters region of the Paria River resulted in a flow downstream. The Paria River Near Kanab, Utah gauge indicated a rise from 5 CFS to over 520 CFS in a span of 10 minutes, and peaked at 842 CFS, with a rise of over 2 feet.
Heavy rainfall caused the low water area on Selmore road to become flooded and impassable.
Temple Bar Rd was closed from Hwy 93 to mile marker 8.
Nipton Rd was washed out just east of I-15.
Yates Well Rd was flooded five feet deep near I-15.

Heavy rain in Utah caused a flash flood in the Paria River that drains into Arizona and the Colorado River near Lees Ferry. The river gauge near on the Paria River near the Colorado River peaked at 6.8 feet at 600 AM.
The little North Fork River at Thornfield reached flood stage impacting the low water crossing. The river rose four feet in a short period of time.
A COOP Observer measured 6.20 inches of rain.
Heavy rainfall of 1.1 inches.

events.narrative: Broadcast media relayed a report of a waterspout in Terrebonne Bay southeast of Cocodrie.
The river gauge on Granite Creek showed a rise of 2.55 feet in 90 minutes (at 1130 AM).  Flooding was reported on Highway 69 near milepost 295.
Flooding was reported at the intersection of North Roberston and Kentucky Street.
Flooding was reported at the intersection of Pace Boulevard and General Meyer Avenue.
Heavy rain over the Pipeline, Tunnel, and Schultz Fire scars caused flash flooding that closed Highway 89 in both directions from mile marker 426 to 434.
Flash flooding and a significant debris flow occurred over the Pack Creek Fire burn scar as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms.
A video showed a wash flowing over a low water crossing along 48th Street, making the road impassable. No damage or injuries were reported.
Heavy rainfall of 1.54 inches.

Areas downstream of the Pack Creek Fire burn scar experienced flash flooding as a result of heavy rains over the fire. This included Old City Park Road south of Moab, which had to close due to flooding.

Areas downstream of the Pack Creek Fire burn scar experienced flash flooding as a result of heavy rains over the fire. This included Sunny Acres Lane north of Spanish Valley, which had to close due to flooding.

Mud and debris flowed across County Road 17 at Corbett Creek near the Dallas Trailhead as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms. The Corbett Creek culvert was completely plugged. The road was closed for several hours due to cleanup operations.
Rainfall of 0.54 inch. Mesonet station FW6884 Pine Cove water office.
Rain of 1.58 inch. Mesonet Station HBRC1 Heart Bar at 6800 feet.
Rainfall of 0.8 inch. Mesonet station CVNC1 Seven Oaks.
Thunderstorm winds downed power lines near Drexel and Calle Santa Cruz and downed large tree branches near Snyder and Bear Canyon Rds.
County comms reported several trees blown down between Hartwell and Nuberg.
County comms reported two trees blown down on the northwest side of Anderson.
Ham radio operator reported nickel size hail fell at the intersection of Clemson Highway and Salem Church Rd.
Thunderstorm winds downed a large tree near Tangerine and Lon Adams Rds.

Ham radio operator and county comms reported multiple trees blown down west of Powdersville, including in the area around Smoak Dr, Cely Rd, and Circle Rd. One tree fell on a mobile home, briefly trapping residents inside.
A power pole and two power lines were blown down.
Around 1 of heavy rain in less an 1 hour caused Valley View Wash to flood N. Flecha Dr. as well as River Rd. between Swan and Pontatoc Rds. in the Catalina Foothils.
Flash flooding closed numerous roads in and south of Golden Valley.

Heavy rain in the Rio Rancho and Vista Hills areas caused flooding. At a home in Rio Rancho, standing water was reported two inches deep in someone's backyard. In Vista Hills, dirt roads were flooded and arroyos were reported to be running. Damages are estimated.
Stockton Hill Rd was closed.
A trained spotter near Edgewood reported that their home was inundated with water from flash flooding. Damages are estimated.
A mudslide occurred on Colorado Highway 133 near Redstone at mile marker 57 as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms.
A tree was reported down across the road at 1914 Shulerville Road.

Law enforcement reported standing water in downtown Cave Spring due to heavy rainfall producing a rise on nearby Cedar Creek and slow drainage. Radar estimates indicate that between 1.5 and 2 inches of rain fell quickly on top of 1 to 2.5 inches that occurred in the preceding 24-hours.
Images showed significant roof damage to a couple of homes and a flipped trailer home just north of I-8 near Montgomery Road. No injuries were reported.
Multiple toppled or snapped wooden power poles were reported along Rodeo Road west of SR 387. Additional downed power poles were reported along McCartney Road nearby. No injuries were reported.
A tree was downed on Caney Lake Road northwest of Minden.
